title: Insertion Sort
body:
Sort the way you sort a hand of cards. Keep the front of the [[Array]] sorted, take the next
element, and slide it back into position, shifting the larger elements right to make room.
$O(n^2)$ average and worst, but the one $O(n^2)$ sort that earns its place in real code.

```java
void insertionSort(int[] a) {
    for (int i = 1; i < a.length; i++) {
        int key = a[i];
        int j = i - 1;
        while (j >= 0 && a[j] > key) {   // shift right until the gap is right
            a[j + 1] = a[j];
            j--;
        }
        a[j + 1] = key;
    }
}
```

```
[5, 2, 4, 6, 1]   take 2 -> [2, 5, 4, 6, 1]
                  take 4 -> [2, 4, 5, 6, 1]
                  take 6 -> [2, 4, 5, 6, 1]   (no shift needed)
                  take 1 -> [1, 2, 4, 5, 6]
```

## Why it survives

**$O(n)$ on nearly-sorted input.** If each element is already close to where it belongs, the
inner `while` exits almost immediately and the whole thing is one pass. Nothing else in the
$O(n \log n)$ family does that, because they do their $\log n$ levels of work regardless.

**Tiny constants.** No recursion, no scratch array, no pivot logic, and a tight inner loop
that walks memory in order. On small arrays (roughly 10 to 20 elements) it beats
[[Quick Sort]] and [[Merge Sort]] outright, which is why real library sorts are hybrids:
they recurse down with quick sort or merge sort and hand the small subarrays to insertion
sort.

**Online.** It can sort data as it arrives, since the front of the array is valid at every
step.

| | |
|---|---|
| Time | $O(n)$ best (sorted), $O(n^2)$ average and worst (reversed) |
| Space | $O(1)$, in place |
| Stable | yes, the `>` in the shift test never moves equal elements past each other |

Against [[Bubble Sort]], which has the same complexity: insertion sort shifts instead of
swapping, so it does about a third of the writes, and it is the one to reach for.
